data.title: Hitachi Energy plans to build C$479M transformer insulation factory in Ontario
data.description:
Hitachi Energy (HTHIY) (HTHIF) said Friday it plans to spend C$479M (US$337.7M) to build a new, state-of-the-art transformer insulation factory in London, Ontario, aiming to strengthen domestic manufacturing and North America's transformer supply chain.

The facility will feature Canada's first pressboard manufacturing line and Hitachi Energy's (HTHIY) (HTHIF) first in the Americas, bringing production of a critical transformer insulation material closer to the North American market, the company said.

The project is backed by C$50M in combined federal and provincial government support, comprised of C$20M from Ottawa's Strategic Response Fund, C$20M from the Invest Ontario Fund, and C$10M from Natural Resources Canada.

Hitachi Energy (HTHIY) (HTHIF) said the London facility is part of its commitment to invest more than $2B to bolster the North American supply chain through 2027; other recent investments in Canada include the acquisition of transformer insulation manufacturer Canduct and a C$270M expansion to nearly triple large power transformer production in Quebec.

data.title: UK proposes 'strategic market status' for Microsoft; final decision set for February
data.description:
Following months of investigation, the U.K.'s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed to designate Microsoft (MSFT) with "strategic market status" regarding its business software ecosystem.

"SMS designation does not find or assume wrongdoing," the decision reads. "Instead, it is the gateway into the UK's digital markets competition regime. It enables the CMA to take action aimed at promoting competition in technology sectors that are key to UK consumers, businesses and the economy."

The CMA will now conduct consultation through November 13, and it will issue a final decision on the proposed designation by Feb. 13, 2027.

"We welcome the CMA's acknowledgement that Microsoft's market position in cloud does not justify a Digital Markets Competition Regime designation but do not share the CMA's views in its proposed decision on business software solutions," a Microsoft spokesperson said to Seeking Alpha. "All our products—including Copilot—are open and interoperable, giving customers the ability to use them alongside competing services and choose solutions that work best for them at attractive prices. We will continue engaging constructively to ensure UK customers and businesses carry on benefiting from robust competition."

The CMA concludes in its report that Microsoft's broad suite of business software products work well together, and its bundling options offer enterprise-wide discounts for customers.

"A broad range of UK customers tell us that these commercial and integration benefits are an important driver for their decision to buy Microsoft business software products," the CMA said. "This has allowed Microsoft to use a position of strength with customers in one product area to expand into others. As an example, Microsoft added security products to the bundles that included its productivity software applications, as security grew in importance for business software customers."

However, they also concluded that the success of its bundling efforts makes it difficult for competitors.

"Even rivals who offer products across more than one digital activity face challenges in winning customers from Microsoft," the report noted. "Their narrower product range, disadvantages due to network effects and significant customer switching costs limit their ability to compete for existing Microsoft customers, many of which are large enterprises."

If the CMA confirms the designation, its actions include supporting customer choice and enabling innovation. These might attempt to ensure Microsoft's commercial arrangements do not limit competition or that effective user choice is not undermined through Microsoft's design of user interfaces.

data.title: BofA says memory chip stock selloff looks overdone
data.description:
The recent drop in memory chip stocks does not match the health of the business, according to analysts at Bank of America. 

"The recent correction in memory stocks appears largely disconnected from memory fundamentals and reflects excessive concern over an AI-memory boom-bust cycle," BofA analysts said. 

Shares of SK Hynix (SKHY) and Samsung Electronics (SSNLF) have each fallen more than 50% from their June highs over about 3.5 months. Based on 2027-28 earnings forecasts, both trade at 2 to 3 times earnings. In past upswings, the figure was 4 to 7 times.

BofA expects strong prices, sales, and profit margins through 2028. It said 2028 earnings per share could dip by a single-digit percentage but stay near record levels.SK Hynix is likely to give a strong outlook for the fourth quarter on Oct. 28, including a special cash dividend. Taiwan’s Nanya Technology has already issued a positive fourth-quarter forecast. The bank also pointed to monthly PC memory contract price increases of 15% or more and steady spot prices.

"We met Singapore-based investors this week. Feedback on the memory cycle was mixed: hedge fund investors were bearish, while most long-term investors remained bullish," BofA added. The worries included high borrowing costs at AI cloud companies, rising memory supply from China, and slower AI spending.

data.title: Southwest Airlines Q3 setup: Guidance faces earnings-revision test
data.description:
Southwest Airlines (LUV) is set to report third-quarter 2026 results on October 21 after the market closes. Wall Street expects non-GAAP EPS of $0.57 and revenue of $8.24B, but earnings expectations have weakened, with 16 downward EPS revisions versus two upward revisions over the past three months.

The shares traded near $41.15 on Friday, leaving the stock down 0.80% year to date, compared with a 13.13% gain for the S&P 500 (SP500).

Revenue growth and fuel costs are the key factors to watch, with adjusted unit revenue rising 20.1% YoY. For the third quarter, management expects adjusted unit revenue growth of 17.5%–19.5%, supported by its commercial overhaul, including bag fees and assigned seating.

Fuel remains a major risk. The second-quarter fuel costs rose to $3.92 per gallon from $2.32 a year earlier, adding $889M in expenses and creating a $1.17-per-share adjusted earnings headwind.

Management expects third-quarter fuel costs of $3.70–$3.75 per gallon and adjusted non-fuel unit cost growth of 3.5%–4.0%.

Southwest Airlines' third quarter adjusted EPS guidance of $0.50–$0.75 brackets the $0.57 consensus. However, management cut its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to $3.25–$4.25 from at least $4.00, making earnings delivery a key focus.

Seeking Alpha’s Quant system rates the stock 'hold' at 3.11, with A+ grades for valuation and growth, C+ grades for profitability and momentum, and D+ for revisions. 

On the other hand, Seeking Alpha analyst Jaden Mealy maintains a Buy rating, citing Southwest’s commercial transformation and pricing gains, while flagging fuel and execution risks.

Investors will watch whether stronger revenue can offset fuel and operating costs and help stabilize earnings expectations.

data.title: Commercial banking is showing signs of modest expansion – Janney’s Guy LeBas
data.description:
Commercial banking is showing signs of moving from a "no hire/no fire" holding pattern toward modest expansion, according to Guy LeBas, chief fixed income strategist at Janney Montgomery Scott.

In his quarterly summary of third-quarter bank earnings, LeBas noted that business borrowing appears to be accelerating without a corresponding deterioration in credit quality, calling the overall outlook “constructive” for growth.

Consumer spending remains robust across major card issuers, with year-over-year growth running in the high-single to low-double digits, the strategist reported.

JPMorgan (JPM) posted 10% spending growth, Bank of America (BAC) saw 8%, and Citigroup (C) recorded 11%, while charge-offs and delinquencies moved in the opposite direction.

"Consumer net charge-off rates averaged about 0.9% in 3Q and declined sequentially at all three major card banks," he said, adding that it's "hard to find a consumer slowdown in those numbers, though inflation clouds the story a bit."

Regional banks (KRE) are demonstrating similar positive trends, according to LeBas. PNC (PNC), U.S. Bancorp (USB), and M&T (MTB) are each looking at approximately 10% year-over-year commercial loan expansions, he noted.

Adjusted total net charge-off rates across regionals, including USB (USB), PNC (PNC), Truist (TFC), Regions (RF), and M&T (MTB), averaged about 0.36% in the third quarter—"a pretty benign number this far into an expansion, particularly given the level of interest rates," the analyst said.

Credit quality indicators remain encouraging despite increased lending activity, LeBas observed.

While there are "scattered blemishes," criticized and nonperforming trends generally aren't flashing warning signs, and Bank of America (BAC), USB (USB), and Regions (RF) all saw declining criticized exposure despite higher volumes, according to his analysis.

The broad message from third-quarter bank earnings is that consumers are spending, businesses are increasingly willing to borrow, and neither group is showing much evidence of trouble paying it back, the strategist concluded.

However, he cautioned that this positive trajectory may be "less helpful for anyone waiting for demand destruction to solve the Fed's inflation problem."

Bank ETFs: (KBWB), (KBE), and (FTXO).

Regional Bank ETFs: (KRE), (KBWR), (IAT), and (DPST).

data.title: Hedge fund Two Sigma ends real estate unit fundraising, cuts staff - report
data.description:
Quantitative hedge fund Two Sigma Investments has halted efforts to raise $2B for its real estate investment unit and cut senior staff, as rising interest rates hobbled its fundraising efforts, according to a media report on Friday.

The unit's partner and chief investment officer, Rich Gomel, is leaving the company. Others on the real estate leadership team, including two of the three remaining partners and one of the two heads of data science, are also departing, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The firm, which had targeted raising ~$2B for the business, pulled in less than half that amount, some of the people told Bloomberg. Some of the real estate team will remain to manage its existing portfolio of properties.

Rising interest rates have weighed on commercial property valuations and led to owners holding assets for longer. Bloomberg, citing data from PEI Group, noted that private real estate fundraising totaled just over $30B for Q3 2026, the lowest quarterly total since early 2013.

Two Sigma started forming the real estate business in 2019 and launched it with internal capital about two years later. It was led by former Blackstone Vice Chair Tom Hill, who left the firm last year, one of the people told Bloomberg.

The business started taking outside capital in 2024 with its Real Estate Opportunity Fund, which mostly focused on housing and industrial investments, with some selective stakes in hospitality and office real estate. The hedge fund's strategy was to use the firm's data to power predictive tools that could project supply and demand, which would determine investment decisions.

Biggest stock movers Friday: Chips stocks, CRWV, and more
data.description:
Stock futures were mixed on Friday as Wall Street builds on the prior session's recovery from an earlier AI-driven tech sell-off, pointing to a positive finish for the week.

Here are some of Friday's biggest stock movers:

Biggest stock gainers

  • SITE Centers (SITC) +18% - Shares surged after the retail real estate investment trust announced plans to voluntarily delist its common shares from the New York Stock Exchange following a special distribution declared on Oct. 15, 2026. The company expects the delisting to take effect before trading begins on Dec. 4, 2026, and said it has not arranged for its shares to trade on another exchange or quotation platform.
  • Cohen & Steers (CNS) +2% - Shares climbed following the release of mixed Q3 results, with total revenue rising 11% Y/Y. The quarter was propelled by $1.6B in broad-based net inflows, representing the strongest quarterly inflow performance since the fourth quarter of 2021, though total assets under management closed at $95.9B, down 4.2% sequentially due to $5.1B in market depreciation. Growth was bolstered by continued momentum across wealth channels, including mutual funds, SICAVs, and the newly launched Cohen & Steers Real Assets Active ETF (CSRA).

Biggest stock losers

  • Omeros (OMER) -12% - Shares plummeted after the European Medicines Agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) issued a second negative opinion on the marketing authorization application for its stem cell transplant therapy, narsoplimab. The decision followed a formal re-examination of an initial negative opinion adopted in June. Seattle-based Omeros noted that patient-level data submitted in August was excluded from the ad hoc expert panel’s reevaluation, despite meeting minutes recommending an external expert review of that data. Narsoplimab, marketed in the U.S. as Yartemlea for stem cell transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy, continues its U.S. commercial rollout. Separately, Omeros announced plans to wind down its European compassionate-use program to prioritize escalating U.S. commercial demand.
  • CoreWeave (CRWV) -5% - Shares slipped despite Cantor Fitzgerald encouraging investors to "buy the dip." Cantor analyst Brett Knoblauch reiterated an Overweight rating and a $176 price target, dismissing recent market concern over CoreWeave's leverage as excessive fearmongering. Knoblauch emphasized that CoreWeave's hardware revenue capacity has nearly doubled to $20 million per megawatt with 25–30% contribution margins, compressing payback cycles on GPU investments to 2–2.5 years. However, investor anxiety remains heightened following a 15% debt-fueled equity plunge earlier in the week, compounded by a Gartner research report forecasting that 80% of independent neocloud providers could cease standalone operations by 2030 due to capital intensity.
  • Micron (MU) -3% - Semiconductor equities slid across the board Friday, threatening to extend the sector's losing streak to an eighth consecutive session as persistent fears over high borrowing costs and AI infrastructure spending drag down high-beta tech names. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell nearly 1%, led lower by memory and hardware heavyweights including Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) and SanDisk (SNDK), which dropped 3% each. Broad-based selling hit chipmakers across the board, with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Broadcom (AVGO), Lam Research (LRCX), and Intel (INTC) each shedding 2% as institutional investors continued trimming risk exposure across logic and hardware suppliers.
